runs.text: pera defenſão, ou pera ter o encontro dos ini-

lines.note: Continues the preceding page's military definition: for defence or to withstand the enemy's onset. The context and the cross-stroked f support defenſão rather than the OCR deſenſão; ini- continues below.
Migos completes inimigos, the enemies whose attack is to be resisted. The short continuation is an ordinary body row.
Teawase is the meeting or encounter of two military formations. The visible c in Encontro corrects OCR Entontro.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Vnião, ou a juntamento dos de hũa

lines.note: The second sense is union or coming together of those on one side and the other. The paragraph sign omitted by the draft is visible at the left; the printed separation in a juntamento is retained.
Completes the two-sided gathering: those of one party and of the other. It belongs to Teauaxe rather than starting a separate entry.
Teayamachi denotes a mishap caused by the hands or an inadvertent act. The usage explanation begins here; deſta, with its visible t, corrects deſa.

runs.text: palaura quando ſe queima algũa caſa por deſa-

lines.note: The word is used when a house burns accidentally. The final deſa- joins the following physical line; the tilde remains over the printed u in algũa.
Completes deſaſtre, the accidental mishap in the house-fire example. This brief ending closes Teayamachi.
Tebako is a small box or casket, as the two Portuguese nouns explain. The capital is T, matching the alphabetical run; OCR rebaco misread its damaged upper strokes.

runs.text: O aſoarſe com a mão. Vt,

lines.note: Tebana denotes blowing one's nose using the hand. The example starts Teba and continues on the following row; the dot-like terminal mark is retained rather than supplied as a hyphen.
Together with Teba above, this gives tebana wo kamu, blowing the nose in this manner. The final B is the upright low-register usage label, not italic Portuguese text.
Tebatebaxij is applied to a flatterer or someone trying to please. The relative clause continues below and establishes the interpersonal sense of the adjective.
Completes the description as pleasing others with gentle, sweet words. The printed palauras and historical spelling are retained.
The example, tebatebashii ishoo wo kiru, introduces wearing conspicuous or inappropriate clothing. The caron over the long vowel in ixǒ is visible, while Vestir retains the baseline st treatment.

runs.text: veſtido que não he proporcionado à qualidade

lines.note: The garment does not correspond to the wearer's quality or social standing. This qualifies the clothing example, not the preceding flattering speech.

runs.text: da peßoa por via da cor, ou pintura extraua-

lines.note: Explains the mismatch through colour or extravagant decoration. The scan supports extraua- rather than OCR exiraua-, continuing to -gante below.
Gante completes extraua-gante, describing the colour or decoration that makes the garment unsuitable. The entry ends on this short row.

runs.text: O ſer muito eſperto, & eſpedito ẽ

lines.note: Tebashikai describes being alert and quick at practical tasks. The visible t in eſperto corrects the OCR vowel-like stroke; eſpedito retains its historical spelling.

runs.text: fazer as couſas, & juntamente riſpido, & ſa-

lines.note: The description combines readiness in doing things with a brisk, somewhat brusque manner. The divided ſa- belongs to ſacadido below, whose historical form is not modernized.
Completes ſacadido and exemplifies tebashikai hito, a person of this sort. The apparent printed ceſ- is retained although the intended Portuguese construction is deſta laya; its initial type is weak.
Completes the preceding ceſ-ta laya, “of this kind,” referring to the quick, brisk person. The anomalous preceding initial remains recorded in that line rather than silently corrected here.
Tebayai is a person diligent and nimble with the hands. The initial vowel is e, not OCR o; the printed lestes is retained despite its number differing from singular peſſoa.
Tebayana is an adjectival alternative with the same nimble-handed meaning as Tebayai. Idem refers to the preceding gloss.
Tebin is explained by temoto or temawari, the area near one's hands. The visible e in both explanatory forms corrects the OCR Tomoto and tamauari; the Portuguese gloss continues below.
Completes the sense of being at hand. Tebin ni wa nai is the negative example, translated beginning with Não; the Japanese niwa sequence is left in the source's joined spelling.
Completes the translation, “I do not have it here at hand now.” The temporal agora explains practical availability in the preceding example.

runs.text: Obater das mãos a compaſſo. Vt,

lines.note: Tebyooshi is beating or clapping the hands in time. The caron is visible over o, and the gloss specifies a regular beat or measure.
Tebyooshi wo utsu is to clap or mark time with the hands. The surviving x and contiguous suffix uo correct the OCR's broken Tebiǒ iuo.

runs.text: Couſa larga, ou eſpaçoſa, como caſa,

lines.note: Tebiroi means broad or spacious, illustrated by a house and, below, a fortress. The Portuguese describes physical extent here before moving to generous expenditure.
After completing the fortress example, tebiroo tsukoo illustrates broad or liberal spending. The circumflex in Tebirô and caron in tçucǒ are distinct visible types.

runs.text: ſtar francamente por muitas partes, ou em mui-

lines.note: Completes Ga-ſtar: spending freely in many places or on many things. The second mui- is physically divided and continues on the next row.
Tas completes muitas couſas, “many things,” closing the explanation of liberal expenditure. It remains a separate physical continuation.

Tebiroo is the adverb corresponding to Tebiroi; tebiro-sa names breadth or extensiveness. The visible r corrects Tebitô. The second pass confirms that the descending italic ſ is actually printed within the otherwise upright Japanese nominal form; this local mixed typography is preserved.

Tebiya denotes a firearm. At the far right of this same physical row, the parenthesis and gardas. complete eſpin- in the following Tebiyacaqe entry; the displaced material is preserved in its printed position, not joined into this firearm gloss.

runs.text: Cauides em que poem as eſpin-

lines.note: Tebiyakake is a rack or hooks on which firearms are placed. The final eſpin- is completed by the displaced gardas. printed above at c1-l034; no ordinary continuation row is missing.
Tebiya no kusuri is gunpowder, literally the firearm's powder or preparation. The visible o after u restores printed Poluora rather than OCR Polura.
Tebiya no dai is the stock of a firearm, precisely the Portuguese coronha. The damaged initial repeats the capital T of adjacent entries.
Teboo is a certain short staff or cudgel. The mark over o points downward as a caron; both the damaged T and the Japanese headword's upright type are restored from the scan.
Teboko is explained as a small naginata and compared below with a polearm. The capital T remains identifiable under the diagonal copy mark crossing the margin.
Completes maneira and compares the weapon with a partisan. The historical form partaſana is retained rather than modernizing the European weapon name.

runs.text: Vaſoura de mão ſem pao, ou cabo.

lines.note: Tebooki is a hand broom without a stick or handle. The headword's b and caroned o are visible despite damaged ink, correcting OCR renǒqi; the gloss supports the broom interpretation.

runs.text: O aleuantar o falcão hum pee pera

lines.note: Tebukuro here is a falconry term for a falcon raising one foot. It is not the ordinary glove sense alone; the purpose of the action follows on the next row.

runs.text: o aquentar entre as penas. Vt,

lines.note: The falcon warms its foot among its feathers. Tebucuro- begins the example; the second vowel is e, matching the headword rather than OCR Tobucuro.

runs.text: Puxar pollo pee deſta maneira, ou

lines.note: Tebukuro wo hiku names drawing up the foot in this manner. The damaged initial of fiqu is read as f from its surviving strokes and the coherent Japanese verb; the Portuguese immediately explains the action. The fi types and final e of pee are abraded, so these chosen readings retain a nonblocking graphic caveat.
Completes the action as raising the foot, then introduces a figurative sense. The surviving letter sequence supports aleuantalo rather than OCR ateuarralo.

runs.text: ſe, ou tornar atras com medo, &c. o q̃ eſta-

lines.note: The metaphor is drawing back or retreating in fear. Recolher-ſe crosses the row boundary, and tornar corrects the OCR's rornar; the relative clause begins o q̃ eſta-.

runs.text: ua pera ſair, ou pera fazer algũa couſa.

lines.note: Completes eſta-ua: someone who was about to go out or do something draws back. The reading retains the divided historical Portuguese spelling and closes the falconry metaphor.
Tebune is a boat for one's own use. The Portuguese explains personal use directly, without specifying a particular type of vessel.

runs.text: Eſcoteiro que vai bulindo com os bra-

lines.note: Teburi first describes someone going unburdened and swinging the arms. The Portuguese bra- begins braços on the following row.
Completes braços and explains carrying nothing. Teburi de mai- begins the example of going in this manner.

runs.text: Ir desta maneira. ¶ Item, Modo de

lines.note: Ru completes mairu, the example of going empty-handed. The entry then turns to a second sense: the manner of hand movement.

runs.text: bulir, ou menear as mãos. Vt,

lines.note: Explains moving or gesturing with the hands and begins te-buri ga in the example. The roman Japanese resumes after italic Vt.
Completes teburi ga yoi or warui hito, a person with good or bad hand gestures. The Portuguese verb is tem, with a damaged final m, rather than OCR teni.

runs.text: ou ruim meneo, ou postura das mãos.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the good-or-bad contrast as movement or posture of the hands. The historical word meneo is preserved.

Tekagami is a bound collection of model handwriting specimens. Encadena continues as dos below; the small terminal dot-like mark is retained provisionally as in the aligned OCR and is not inferred from the word division.

runs.text: dos de letra boa de homẽs antigos, & inſignes.

lines.note: Completes encadenados and describes fine handwriting by ancient, distinguished people. The clearly visible final word is inſignes, correcting the OCR's inſignti.
Tekake is glossed as a mistress or concubine. The capital T corrects the OCR r without altering the Japanese q spelling.
Tekaki denotes a good writer or calligrapher. The Portuguese eſcriuão supplies the professional or skilled-writing sense; the initial T is restored.
Tekkai here denotes armour for the arms. The gloss concerns the arms as body parts, distinct from the following homographic disability term.

runs.text: Braço, ou mão aleijada, ou encolhida.

lines.note: This separate Tekkai entry concerns a disabled or contracted arm or hand. The scan supports encolhida, replacing the malformed OCR eneohida.

The dictionary gives chokkai as the expression used in Cami. Cami is a Japanese regional designation embedded in the Portuguese explanation; its printed italic treatment is retained for optional whole-word review.
Tetchuu is explained as kurogane no hashira, an iron pillar. The r in faxira corrects OCR faxita, and the mark over u is a visible caron.
Ferro completes “column of iron.” The two r types correct ferto, while the upright S is the written-register label rather than part of the italic gloss.

Tekogi, alternatively takogi, is a lever. The initial capital is not securely distinguishable by typeface in this impression, so its baseline italic marking is retained; the remaining Japanese letters are upright.

runs.text: Couſa muita em quantidade, ou grãde.

lines.note: Tekoi describes something abundant in quantity or great in degree. The Portuguese makes the broad quantitative meaning explicit before the striking example.
Tekoo yamasuru is rendered as giving many blows. The phrase illustrates intensity, with the circumflex retained on the adverb Tecô.
Completes “giving many blows to someone.” The short object phrase belongs wholly to the preceding example.
Tekoo is separately listed as the adverb of Tecoi. Adu. is italic grammatical apparatus and does not provide a new lexical sense.
Tekka is explained by iron and fire and glossed as heated or glowing iron. The scan prints Curogane fi without adding an expected linking particle.

Tecqeô is explained as iron chopsticks or a small iron skewer. The damaged letter before ô is read as e rather than OCR t; Faxis is the Japanese utensil word used within the Portuguese explanation. The supplied NINJAL headword index subsequently corroborates the independently read Tecqeô.

runs.text: de ferro ſobre q̃ aſão algũa couſa metendo bra-

lines.note: The iron support or skewer is used to roast something, with glowing coals placed underneath. The abbreviated q̃ and divided bra- remain literal.
Completes bra-ſas: embers placed below the iron roasting utensil. The physically separate de baixo is retained.
Tekki is explained as iron's qi or nature, with shoo as an alternative. The Japanese explanatory terms are upright and outside the Portuguese gloss; Qualida- continues below.

runs.text: de, ou natureza de ferro. Vt,

lines.note: Completes “quality or nature of iron.” Tekki wo imu describes avoiding contact with iron; the legible m corrects the OCR intu.

runs.text: Mezinha que ſe dana ſe lhe tocão

lines.note: Kusuri completes the example of a medicine that must avoid iron. The Portuguese states that the preparation is spoiled if touched with it.

Com ferro completes the warning about iron contact. Separately at the far right, the parenthesis and de ferro. qualify the small bow in the following Tecqiǔ entry; the OCR merged and garbled this displaced fragment.
Tekkyuu is an iron bow, explained by kurogane no yumi. Its Portuguese “small bow” is completed by de ferro. printed above at c2-l029; the physical displacement is preserved.
Tekubi is the wrist. The Portuguese calls it the “neck of the hand,” an anatomical paraphrase rather than a separate sense of the Japanese word.

runs.text: Coua que està na palma da mão.

lines.note: Tekubo denotes the hollow in the palm. Coua and the grave-accented està retain the historical Portuguese forms; the st allograph follows the aligned baseline.

runs.text: O fazer andar às voltas, ou me-

lines.note: Tegugutsu denotes working or moving puppets. The gloss begins making them turn around or move; the scan has a word space in fazer andar that the OCR omitted.
Completes me-near os bonifratres, moving the puppets. The full continuation is legible in the scan and replaces the OCR's unrelated garble; bonifratres retains the printed internal r sequence.
Tedaimatsu is a hand torch made from a small bundle of wood. The Portuguese diminutive describes tied pieces or splinters, with the alternative completed below.
Completes the bundle as small pine chips for lighting. Cauaquinhos preserves the historical spelling rather than modernizing it.
Tedate is a Japanese shield or buckler. The initial in Iapão is capital I, correcting OCR tapão; this is the Portuguese country name, not a Japanese term for typeface toggling.
The second Tedate is a device, stratagem, or deception. Its separate entry distinguishes this abstract sense from the shield above.
Tedate wo suru exemplifies devising or employing a stratagem. The Japanese phrase is upright after the italic example marker.

runs.text: O tomar viuo a alguem. Vt,

lines.note: Tedori is taking someone alive. The example begins So-, which continues as sono on the following line.
Completes sono hito wo tedori ni shite kurei, a request to take that person alive for the speaker. Tomar me begins the Portuguese rendering across the row break.
Completes “take that man alive for me.” Tac. is an upright source citation; the OCR's italic final c is corrected without expanding the source abbreviation.

runs.text: Aſas da panela de ferro do Chanoyu.

lines.note: This separate Tedori denotes the handles of the iron kettle used for chanoyu. Chanoyu is a Japanese term inside the Portuguese explanation, and the headword begins at the ordinary column margin.
Tedouoi describes something far away or beyond easy reach. The visible t restores afaſtada, and the grave over the final a of eſtà is present; no comma is visible after afaſtada at the right rule.

runs.text: pera lhe apontar, ou atirar com arco. ¶ Ite,

lines.note: Specifies distance for aiming at something or shooting with a bow. The scan supports atirar com rather than OCR attrar com, and the following abbreviated Item-like marker is read Ite, without supplying an unseen m.
The additional gloss says something far from the hands. It expresses the same out-of-reach sense independently of the bow example.

runs.text: Hum buraco q̃ tem o capecete na cimeira

lines.note: Tehen is the opening at the top of a helmet. The damaged headword and final cimeira are read from the remaining letterforms and the coherent helmet description; the explanation continues onto the next page.
